source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Part III: Pullbacks: Trends Converting to Trading Ranges

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: PullbackBarStrict
candidates.quote: In the strictest sense, a pullback is a bar that moves against the trend enough to take out the prior bar's extreme. In a bull trend, a pullback is a move where a bar extends at least one tick below the low of the prior bar.
candidates.description: Shared primitive, narrow definition: in a bull trend, the current bar's low is at least one tick below the prior bar's low.

candidates.name: PullbackBarBroad
candidates.quote: a broader definition is more useful, and any pause (including an inside bar, an opposite trend bar, or a doji bar) in a trend's momentum should be considered to be a pullback, even though there may be only sideways action and not an actual move backward
candidates.description: Shared primitive, broad definition: a pause in trend momentum -- the current bar is an inside bar, or a trend bar against the prevailing trend color, or a doji.
candidates.pseudocode: isInsideBar(0) || close[0] < open[0] || isDojiBar(0)  (bull-trend reading; bear trend mirrors with close[0] > open[0])

complexity.reason: single/two-bar OHLC arithmetic once inside-bar and doji primitives exist

notes: Uses the InsideBar and DojiBar primitives from R08 (book-internal) / the trilogy's shared corpus.

candidates.name: TwoLeggedPullback
candidates.quote: Since a pullback is a trend, even though it is usually small compared to the larger trend from which it is pulling back, like all trends it will commonly have at least two legs.
candidates.description: Filter/context: a pullback commonly has two (sometimes one or three) legs; traders fade the breakout of the pullback's first leg and expect the trend to resume only after a second leg.
candidates.pseudocode: legCount(pullback) >= 2  (an ABC move: countertrend leg A, smaller with-trend leg B, second countertrend leg C)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter on when to expect trend resumption)

complexity.reason: leg counting on a pullback has no agreed mechanical definition, as with R08-16's leg counting on a full trend

notes: The book's own hedge: 'oftentimes the two legs are clearly visible only on a smaller time frame chart and have to be inferred.'

candidates.name: DeepRetracementFlipsTrendBias
candidates.quote: the odds that a pullback will get back to the prior trend's extreme fall substantially if the pullback retraces 75 percent or more. For a pullback in a bear trend, at that point, a trader is better off thinking of the pullback as a new bull trend rather than a pullback in an old bear trend.
candidates.description: Filter: once a pullback has retraced at least R percent of the prior leg's range (measured from the leg's start to its extreme), stop treating it as a pullback in the old trend -- treat it as a new trend in the opposite direction instead, so old-trend with-trend signals are no longer favored.
candidates.pseudocode: legStart = lowest(low, legLookback)[e]; legExtreme = highest(high, legLookback)[e]; retracement = (legExtreme - low[0]) / (legExtreme - legStart); retracement >= retracementThreshold

complexity.reason: needs the prior leg's start and extreme to persist across bars, otherwise a plain ratio

candidates.name: MinimumRewardToRiskFilter
candidates.quote: Once they determine their risk, they can then set a profit target that is at least as large as the risk and reasonably assume that they have about a 60 percent chance or better of being successful.
candidates.description: Filter: only take a signal if its planned reward (distance from entry to target) is at least a multiple of its planned risk (distance from entry to protective stop).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (trade-selection filter, applied before placing the entry order)

complexity.reason: a plain comparison of two already-known distances

notes: Restates the general 'trader's equation' Brooks applies throughout the trilogy; the 60 percent figure itself is not separately testable from bars.

candidates.name: MicroChannel
candidates.quote: The final leg of a pullback is often a micro channel against the trend (a bear micro channel at the end of a bull flag or a bull micro channel at the end of a bear flag). ... especially if the micro channel has four or more bars.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: over the last N bars, each bar's body is the same color and consecutive bars overlap only slightly (a tight, small-tailed channel), with N at or above a minimum length to count as significant.
candidates.pseudocode: for i in 0..microChannelBars-2: close[i] < open[i] && (min(high[i], high[i+1]) - max(low[i], low[i+1])) <= overlapFraction * (high[i+1] - low[i+1])  (bear micro channel; bull mirrors on close[i] > open[i])

complexity.reason: fixed-length loop of two-bar overlap and color checks, akin to R08-18's thin area

candidates.name: MicroChannelBreakoutEntry
candidates.quote: If the trend is strong, there is often no pullback and therefore entering on the breakout of the micro channel is a reasonable trade.
candidates.description: In a strong trend, enter on a stop beyond the extreme of a bear MicroChannel (buy) when it breaks with a with-trend bar, without waiting for a further pullback.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the micro channel's high

complexity.reason: depends on the MicroChannel window plus a breakout test

notes: Companion filter: the book prefers this only when 'the underlying trend is strong' -- see RP3-13.

candidates.name: PauseBarBreakoutEntry
candidates.quote: if there is a strong bull move in which the last bar was a small bar with a high just a tick or two below the prior bar's high and that bar was a large bull trend bar and followed one or two other large bull trend bars, if you buy one tick above this bar, you are buying at the high of the day.
candidates.description: In the early stages of a strong trend (one or more large trend bars just occurred), buy a stop one tick above a small pause bar whose high sits within a few ticks of the prior bar's high (a 'high 1' entry).
candidates.pseudocode: LargeTrendBar[1] && high[0] < high[1] && (high[1] - high[0]) <= pauseTicks * tickSize && (high[0] - low[0]) <= pauseBarMaxRange * (high[1] - low[1])
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the pause bar's high

complexity.reason: cross-bar comparison plus the LargeTrendBar primitive

notes: This is the trilogy's 'high 1' pattern, formalized more fully in Chapter 17 (bar counting H1/H2/L1/L2); recorded here since it first appears in this chapter.

candidates.name: FollowThroughBarConfirmsReversal
candidates.quote: What they need to see is follow-through selling in the form of maybe just one more bear trend bar. ... If the bar instead has a bull close, they will suspect that the reversal attempt has failed and that the sell-off is just a brief, but sharp, markdown in price and therefore a buying opportunity.
candidates.description: Filter: after a potential reversal (one or two strong bars against the established trend), require the very next bar to also close in the new direction before treating the always-in trend as flipped; a with-trend-colored next bar means the move was only a pullback.
candidates.pseudocode: potentialReversalBars(bodyFraction) >= 1 && close[0] < open[0]  (confirms a bear reversal is genuine); close[0] > open[0] on that next bar instead treats it as a pullback in the still-intact bull trend
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter deciding reversal vs. pullback)

complexity.reason: needs the preceding potential-reversal bar(s) plus a same-direction confirmation test on the following bar

candidates.name: TrailingStopBelowRecentSwingLow
candidates.quote: If the market makes a new high, they will raise their stops to below the most recent higher low.
candidates.description: In a bull trend, trail the protective stop to just below the most recent confirmed swing low each time a new trend high forms.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] > highest(high, lookback)[1] -> stopPrice = lowestSwingLow(pivotStrength) - bufferTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection plus persistence of the trailed stop level

notes: Not TrailingStop from the catalog (that trails by a dollar/ATR amount off peak profit); this trails to a structural swing level instead.

candidates.name: ExitOnSecondWithTrendResumptionAttemptFailure
candidates.quote: one of the cardinal rules about trading reversals is to exit on the market's second attempt to resume the trend.
candidates.description: Exit a position held in the old trend direction once the market's second attempt to resume that trend fails (e.g. a second high-2/low-2-style resumption attempt is rejected), since a second failed attempt raises the odds the trend has genuinely reversed.

complexity.reason: counting 'attempts to resume the trend' requires the same pivot/leg-counting design decision as TwoLeggedPullback

candidates.name: BreakoutPullbackAfterStrongChannelBreak
candidates.quote: When a channel is steep, it is better not to enter a reversal trade on the breakout through the trend line and instead wait to see if there is a breakout pullback that sets up a second signal. ... The test can be a lower high, a double top, or a higher high.
candidates.description: When a trend channel is too steep/tight to trade its first trend-line breakout, skip that first breakout and instead wait for a pullback that retests the channel's extreme (a lower high, double top, or higher high in a bull channel) and take the reversal signal that forms there.
candidates.pseudocode: SteepChannel[b] (channel identified over channelBars ending at breakout bar b) && close[0] < trendLine[0] (breakout bar b) && high[i] retests within retestTicks of high[b] for some i in (b, b+retestWindow] && bearReversalBar[i]
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop below the retest bar's low

complexity.reason: needs channel-steepness classification, trend-line projection, and a persisted retest window

notes: This is the chapter's central worked example (Figure PIII.3, bars 2/4, 6, 8-9/11, 12-14/16, 17/20, 21/23) and is formalized further in the next chapter (First Pullback Sequence).

candidates.name: StrongTrendPrefersMarketEntryOverPullbackWait
candidates.quote: This is important for traders who are waiting to enter on pullbacks. When the trend is strong, it is often better to enter at the market than to wait for a pullback.
candidates.description: Filter: once a trend has shown N consecutive same-direction closes with minimal overlap, favor entering at the market (or on minimal one/two-tick dips) each bar over waiting for a conventional pullback, since a pullback may not come until the trend is much further extended.
candidates.book_order_type: market order or a shallow limit a tick or two below the market

complexity.reason: a fixed-length consecutive-bar count, once trend-bar classification exists

notes: The AAPL walkthrough (p86-87) is an expected-value illustration of the trader's equation, not an independent mechanical test.

candidates.name: TradingRangeInTrendFavorsWithTrendBreakout
candidates.quote: Since a trading range in a bull trend is just a bull flag on a higher time frame chart, the odds favor an upside breakout.
candidates.description: Filter: while price is inside a trading range that formed within an established larger trend, weight breakout attempts in the direction of that larger trend more favorably than countertrend fades.
candidates.pseudocode: inTradingRange(rangeLookback) && largerTrendDirection == bull -> prefer long breakouts over short fades

complexity.reason: requires both a trading-range detector and a larger-trend-direction detector, each itself a design decision

rejected.quote: There will be repeated attempts by the bulls to resume the trend and by the bears to reverse the trend, and 80 percent of both fail.
rejected.reason: narrative probability figure with no independent bar-computable threshold of its own; used only as motivation for the filters already recorded (RP3-03, RP3-14)

rejected.quote: if AAPL is up $4.00 at $280 and it has gone up for seven straight bars ... there is probably about a 70 percent chance that AAPL will go two or three dollars higher before it pulls back one dollar
rejected.reason: a worked expected-value illustration (specific instrument, specific dollar amounts) rather than a generalizable bar-level rule; the underlying mechanical piece is captured by RP3-13

rejected.quote: Once the market gets close to the key price, the vacuum effect often dominates.
rejected.reason: restates the magnet/reversal-near-key-level idea already captured as R08-14/R08-15 and the Chapter 10 magnet family; no new bar-level test

rejected.quote: Do you really think that is of major importance? Sometimes it is but usually close is close enough.
rejected.reason: discretionary philosophical aside about tolerance near a level, not itself a decidable condition (the toleranceTicks parameter pattern used throughout the corpus already covers this)

rejected.quote: Figure PIII.1 ... Figure PIII.2 ... Figure PIII.3
rejected.reason: worked chart examples narrating already-recorded patterns (low 2, high 2, ioi, outside bar, breakout pullback, micro channel) with specific bar numbers; no additional mechanical content beyond RP3-08/09/12

chapter_summary: Part III's introduction is almost entirely discursive: it explains WHY pullbacks happen (profit-taking math, the trader's equation, the 60/80-percent directional-probability framing) and works through several chart examples (Figures PIII.1-PIII.3) illustrating that every pullback begins with a reversal and that breakouts of steep/strong channels should be faded only on a second-chance retest. The genuinely mechanical yield is a pair of pullback-bar primitives (strict and broad), a micro-channel primitive with its breakout entry, a pause-bar ('high 1') entry, a deep-retracement bias flip at 75 percent, a reward:risk trade filter, a structural trailing stop, and the chapter's centerpiece -- BreakoutPullbackAfterStrongChannelBreak, generalizing the many worked examples of waiting for a retest before trading a steep channel's break. Several filters (TwoLeggedPullback, ExitOnSecondWithTrendResumptionAttemptFailure, TradingRangeInTrendFavorsWithTrendBreakout) are graded research because they depend on leg-counting or trading-range/trend identification with no agreed mechanical definition, matching the treatment of similar concepts in Chapter 8.
